period_summary: Citations are densest in the 2nd–4th centuries CE, driven almost entirely by the apologetic and christological use of the 'they shall look on him whom they pierced' clause; this concentration reveals that Zech 12:10 was a primary proof-text in early Christian debate about the crucifixion and parousia, making its textual transmission inseparable from christological controversy.

citations.cited_text: καὶ ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν ('and they shall look upon him whom they pierced')
citations.text_form_note: Justin uses ἐξεκέντησαν ('pierced'), which aligns with the LXX rendering (also echoed in John 19:37) rather than the MT's דָּקָרוּ; the preposition εἰς before ὃν closely matches LXX/Theodotion usage, though the surrounding context is paraphrased.
citations.theological_use: Justin employs the verse as a christological proof-text demonstrating that the Hebrew prophets foresaw the crucifixion of Jesus; he deploys it against Trypho to argue that Jewish scripture itself testifies to Christ's suffering and his future recognition at the Parousia.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's citation, our earliest patristic witness, attests a Greek text closer to the LXX/Theodotion tradition and suggests that by the mid-2nd century this rendering was already standard in Christian apologetic circles in Rome.

citations.cited_text: Et aspicient ad eum quem compunxerunt ('And they shall look upon him whom they have pierced')
citations.text_form_note: The Old Latin compunxerunt renders ἐξεκέντησαν rather than the MT's דָּקָרוּ (pierced/stabbed); the syntax 'ad eum quem' mirrors the Greek εἰς ὃν, supporting dependence on a Greek Vorlage aligned with LXX.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses the text to assert continuity between the God of Israel and the God of the New Testament, arguing that the one 'pierced' is none other than the Son who was crucified, countering Marcionite disjunction between Old and New Testaments.
citations.transmission_implication: Irenaeus's Old Latin rendering preserves evidence that the LXX-aligned Greek text was already translated into Latin before 200 CE, confirming the early westward spread of this Greek text form.

citations.cited_text: Et videbunt in quem transfixerunt ('And they shall see him whom they have transfixed/pierced')
citations.text_form_note: Transfixerunt is a slightly different Latin equivalent than compunxerunt (Irenaeus) or the standard ἐξεκέντησαν; it may reflect an independent Old Latin rendering or possibly some contact with the MT root דקר (thrust through), though the overall syntactic shape still follows the LXX-type construction.
citations.theological_use: Tertullian cites the verse polemically against Marcion to prove that the crucified Christ was foretold in the Jewish scriptures and that the Demiurge/Creator God and the Father of Christ are one; he also invokes it in his resurrection treatise to argue for a bodily recognition of Christ.
citations.transmission_implication: The variation between Tertullian's transfixerunt and Irenaeus's compunxerunt suggests a diversity of Old Latin versions in circulation by the early 3rd century, each ultimately derived from a Greek Vorlage in the LXX tradition but with some freedom in Latin lexical choice.

citations.work: Commentary on John (Commentarii in Johannem); also Contra Celsum
citations.chapter_section: Comm. Joh. II.28; Contra Celsum II.34
citations.cited_text: καὶ ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν ('and they shall look upon him whom they pierced'); in the Hexapla he notes Aquila's ἐπέβλεψαν πρὸς ὅν κατωρχήσαντο and Symmachus's variant
citations.text_form_note: Origen preserves both the LXX text (ἐξεκέντησαν) and the Hexaplaric alternatives; he notes Aquila's rendering that better reflects the MT's דָּקָרוּ (stabbed/thrust through), revealing his awareness of multiple text forms; his own citation in the Commentary and Contra Celsum defaults to the LXX/Theodotion form.
citations.theological_use: Origen uses the passage both christologically (identifying the 'pierced one' with the crucified Logos) and eschatologically (arguing that even those who rejected Christ will ultimately behold him at judgment); his Hexaplaric work shows a critical scholarly approach to the passage's varied textual witnesses.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's Hexaplaric notes are uniquely valuable: they confirm that already by the 3rd century multiple competing Greek translations of this verse were known to scholars, implying a complex transmission history with active Jewish-Christian textual rivalry over the verse's wording.

citations.cited_text: καὶ ἐπιβλέψονται πρός με ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν ('and they shall look upon me whom they pierced')
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius notably retains the first-person 'me' (πρός με) which is attested in some LXX manuscripts and reflects the MT's אֵלַי ('to me'), showing a reading closer to the MT in that one element, while ἐξεκέντησαν aligns with LXX/Theodotion rather than Aquila; the combination is characteristic of the LXX-Hexaplaric tradition.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius deploys the verse as a central proof-text in his apologetic demonstration that the Hebrew prophets predicted Christ's crucifixion, explicitly arguing that the divine 'me' in the first person shows the speaker is the divine Logos who was himself pierced.
citations.transmission_implication: Eusebius's retention of the first-person 'me' and his use of the Hexaplaric apparatus suggests that 4th-century Caesarean scholars were working with a more nuanced, Hexapla-informed text, mediating between LXX and MT traditions.

citations.cited_text: ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν ('they shall look upon him whom they pierced')
citations.text_form_note: Cyril's citation follows the standard LXX/Theodotion form with ἐξεκέντησαν and εἰς ὃν; there is no evidence of contact with the Hebrew MT's first-person form or Aquila's alternative rendering.
citations.theological_use: Cyril cites the verse in the context of catechetical instruction about the crucifixion, presenting it as prophetic fulfillment demonstrated by the lance wound of John 19:34–37; he also invokes it eschatologically as a description of Christ's second coming when all will see the crucified one.
citations.transmission_implication: Cyril's straightforward LXX-type citation in a Jerusalem catechetical context confirms that the LXX/Theodotion reading was the liturgically and doctrinally normative text in Palestinian Christian communities by the 4th century.

citations.cited_text: καὶ ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν ('and they shall look upon him whom they pierced')
citations.text_form_note: Chrysostom's citation is verbally identical to the dominant LXX/Theodotion form; the Antiochene tradition consistently uses ἐξεκέντησαν without any sign of influence from the Aquila or Symmachus alternatives, confirming the uniformity of the LXX form in Antiochene exegesis.
citations.theological_use: Chrysostom uses the verse in his Matthean homilies to reinforce the historical reality of the crucifixion against any docetic minimization, and in his Johannine homilies to link the soldier's lance-thrust directly to prophetic fulfillment, emphasizing Jewish culpability for the 'piercing.'
citations.transmission_implication: The Antiochene school's uniform adoption of the LXX form, without Hexaplaric corrections, suggests that the standard ecclesiastical text was well-established in Syria by the late 4th century and that Origen's textual-critical work had limited practical penetration in preaching contexts.

citations.work: Commentary on Zechariah (Commentarii in Zachariam); Epistulae
citations.cited_text: Et aspicient ad me quem confixerunt (Vulgate rendering: 'and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced'); Jerome also notes the Hebrew reads אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר-דָּקָרוּ and discusses the LXX's ἐξεκέντησαν
citations.text_form_note: Jerome's Vulgate rendering 'ad me quem confixerunt' deliberately restores the MT's first-person 'me' (אֵלַי), which many LXX manuscripts had changed to third-person 'him' (εἰς αὐτόν or εἰς ὅν); confixerunt closely renders דָּקָרוּ, and in his commentary Jerome explicitly criticizes the LXX's handling and defends the Hebraica veritas.
citations.theological_use: Jerome uses the passage to demonstrate his translation principle of following the Hebrew text; he also interprets it christologically but insists the first-person 'me' is theologically important as it identifies the divine speaker (God/Christ) with the one pierced, which he sees the LXX as obscuring.
citations.transmission_implication: Jerome's deliberate correction toward the MT represents a decisive moment in Western transmission history, establishing a Vulgate text that diverges from the Old Latin/LXX tradition and preserving the MT's first-person form that most Greek manuscripts had smoothed away.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citations of Zechariah 12:10 up to the 5th century reveal that the dominant text in ecclesiastical use was the LXX/Theodotion form featuring ἐξεκέντησαν and the third-person construction εἰς ὃν rather than the MT's first-person אֵלַי; this is consistent across geographically diverse witnesses from Rome (Justin), Lyon (Irenaeus), Carthage (Tertullian), Caesarea (Eusebius), Jerusalem (Cyril), and Antioch (Chrysostom). Origen's Hexaplaric work stands as the critical exception, demonstrating scholarly awareness of the MT-aligned alternatives offered by Aquila and Symmachus, but this scholarly knowledge did not substantially alter the ecclesiastical citation tradition. Jerome's Vulgate represents a conscious and polemical reassertion of the MT tradition against the LXX, a turning point that introduces significant textual divergence into Western Christianity's scriptural heritage. The variation between the LXX's third-person and the MT's first-person 'me' had profound christological stakes, since the first-person form more directly identifies the divine speaker with the crucified, and the patristic evidence suggests that different theological commitments drove text-form preferences in different contexts.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers almost universally quoted Zechariah 12:10 from the Greek Old Testament (LXX), using the phrase 'they shall look upon him whom they pierced,' and this version became the standard Christian text for centuries. The Hebrew original says 'they shall look upon me,' and the scholar Jerome was almost alone among patristic writers in insisting on restoring this 'me' in his new Latin translation, creating a significant split between Greek-tradition and Latin-tradition churches. This history shows that Christian copying and theological use of this verse shaped which version of the text survived and spread in early church communities.

notable_variants.reading: εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν / 'him whom they pierced' (third person, with ἐξεκέντησαν)
notable_variants.significance: This third-person form differs from the MT's first-person 'me' and represents the dominant LXX/Theodotion tradition; its widespread adoption in Christian apologetics and preaching means it was the most influential single reading in early Christian use of this verse, and it is also the form quoted in John 19:37, cementing its authority.

notable_variants.reading: ad me quem confixerunt / 'upon me whom they pierced' (first person, MT-aligned, Vulgate)
notable_variants.significance: The restoration of the first-person 'me' aligning with the MT is significant because it changes the theological referent — in the MT, God himself speaks as the one pierced — and Jerome's insistence on this reading reflects his Hebraica veritas program and created a lasting divergence between the Vulgate and the Greek ecclesiatical tradition.

notable_variants.reading: Aquila: ἐπέβλεψαν πρὸς ὅν κατωρχήσαντο (those who 'danced over' or 'mocked' him)
notable_variants.significance: Aquila's highly literal rendering of דָּקָרוּ with κατωρχήσαντο (a word meaning to leap/dance over in mockery or to stab) is preserved only through Origen's Hexapla and is otherwise unattested in patristic quotation; it demonstrates the range of Greek translation strategies applied to a theologically charged verb and shows the MT tradition was not entirely suppressed in scholarly circles.

notable_variants.reading: compunxerunt vs. transfixerunt vs. confixerunt (variant Old Latin renderings)
notable_variants.significance: The variety of Latin verbs used to render ἐξεκέντησαν — compunxerunt (Irenaeus), transfixerunt (Tertullian), confixerunt (Jerome) — attests a pluriform Old Latin tradition prior to Jerome's Vulgate standardization, implying multiple independent translations of the same Greek Vorlage circulating in North Africa and the West before 400 CE.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX Third-Person Shift Dominates Pre-Hieronymian Patristic Tradition
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most significant finding of this patristic citation history is that the LXX/Theodotion's third-person 'him whom they pierced' displaced the MT's theologically richer first-person 'me' across virtually all ecclesiastical traditions, almost certainly because John 19:37 had already canonized this form within the New Testament, creating a feedback loop between NT citation and OT textual transmission. Origen's Hexaplaric preservation of Aquila shows the MT tradition was known but not adopted, while Jerome's deliberate MT correction remained a minority tradition in liturgical practice. This suggests that intra-Christian canonical pressure — specifically, the authority of John's Gospel — was a decisive factor shaping which text form of Zech 12:10 survived in active use.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Early Christian writers almost universally used the Greek version of this verse rather than the original Hebrew, largely because the Gospel of John had already quoted it that way, locking in a specific wording; only Jerome, with his insistence on translating from the Hebrew, broke with this trend, but even his Vulgate did not fully displace the Greek-based tradition in church reading and preaching.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis correctly identifies the central textual issue (LXX ἐξεκέντησαν vs. MT דָּקָרוּ, third- vs. first-person) and the broad patristic reception, but several specific citation references and quoted forms require verification and at least one is likely inaccurate.

flagged_claims.claim: Justin Martyr... Dialogue with Trypho ch. 64; cf. ch. 32, 118
flagged_claims.reason: Justin cites Zech 12:10/John 19:37 most prominently in Dial. 14, 32, 64, 118, and 1 Apol. 52. The specific section breakdown is roughly correct but should be verified; ch. 64 is not the most prominent locus (ch. 14 and 32 are stronger).

flagged_claims.claim: Irenaeus... Against Heresies IV.33.11... 'Et aspicient ad eum quem compunxerunt'
flagged_claims.reason: Irenaeus does cite Zech 12:10 in AH IV.33.11, but the exact Latin wording and whether 'compunxerunt' is the verb used should be verified against critical editions (SC); the quotation may be reconstructed rather than directly checked.

flagged_claims.claim: Tertullian... Against Marcion III.7.7; also De Resurrectione Carnis 22... 'Et videbunt in quem transfixerunt'
flagged_claims.reason: Tertullian cites the verse in Adv. Marc. III.7 and Adv. Iud. 14, but the exact section number (III.7.7) and the specific Latin verb 'transfixerunt' need verification; Tertullian's Latin renderings vary across works.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen... Commentary on John II.28; Contra Celsum II.34
flagged_claims.reason: These specific section references are not reliably verifiable for Zech 12:10 citations. Contra Celsum II.34 discusses crucifixion mockery but the Zech 12:10 citation locus needs verification; Comm. Joh. II.28 reference is questionable.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen... notes Aquila's ἐπέβλεψαν πρὸς ὅν κατωρχήσαντο
flagged_claims.reason: Aquila's rendering of דקר here is typically given as something like ἐξεκέντησαν or a related form; κατωρχήσαντο means 'danced in triumph over' and reflects a different Hebrew root (רקד or confusion with דקר). This may conflate Aquila's rendering elsewhere or be a fabricated specific Greek form.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius... Demonstratio Evangelica VI.18; X.7... 'καὶ ἐπιβλέψονται πρός με ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν'
flagged_claims.reason: Eusebius does cite Zech 12:10 in Dem. Ev., but the specific section references (VI.18; X.7) and the precise Greek form quoted need verification against the GCS edition.
Cyril cites Zech 12:10 in Cat. 13 (on the crucifixion); section 13.41 is plausible but the exact paragraph and the citation in Cat. 10.12 require verification.

flagged_claims.claim: John Chrysostom... Hom. 78.2; also Hom. on John 85
flagged_claims.reason: Chrysostom's Matthew homily numbering and specific section (78.2) for a Zech 12:10 citation is not clearly attested; his Hom. on John 85 deals with John 19 but the explicit Zech 12:10 quotation locus needs verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Jerome's Vulgate rendering 'ad me quem confixerunt'
flagged_claims.reason: The Vulgate of Zech 12:10 actually reads 'aspicient ad me quem confixerunt' — this is roughly correct but the precise Vulgate wording should be checked; some editions read 'transfixerunt'.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius's retention of the first-person 'me'... mediating between LXX and MT traditions
flagged_claims.reason: While some LXX manuscripts do read πρός με, the claim that this reflects Hexaplaric mediation in Eusebius specifically is interpretive and stronger than the evidence warrants; πρός με is a known LXX variant independent of Hexaplaric activity.

safe_claims: LXX uses ἐξεκέντησαν while MT reads דָּקָרוּ
John 19:37 echoes the LXX-type form of Zech 12:10
MT has first-person אֵלַי ('to me') while many Greek witnesses read third-person
Zech 12:10 was a major christological proof-text in early Christian apologetics
Jerome's Vulgate generally favors the Hebraica veritas over the LXX
Origen's Hexapla preserved Aquila and Symmachus alternative renderings
The verse was used apologetically against both Jewish and Marcionite interlocutors
